newsitem.title: USA: Devens, Mass., $200 mln development bond debated.
newsitem.headline: Devens, Mass., $200 mln development bond debated.

text.p: Likely to win final approval from the Massachusetts Legislature this week is a measure critical to the continued development of a converted military base into a commerical center.

The bill for Devens Commerce Center raises the ceiling on how much money the Massachusetts Government Land Bank, designated developer of the 4,500-acre former U.S. Army base near the New Hampshire border, may borrow.

The bond authorization is for immediate needs totals $80 million, with another $120 million for long-term needs. The funds are needed to prepare the site for myriad new tenants of the military reservation.
Devens landed on the federal government'sbase-closing list in 1991.

Some 90 miles of roads used for military purposes must be upgraded for commercial use. Water and sewer systems must be brought up to code. Asbestos and lead paint must be removed and buildings demolished. And the state has to pay Washington the $20 million it committed to in purchasing the site.

The federal government retained part of the base and plans to place a federal prison and hospital there, along with a Federal Job Corps training center. Those projects will provide more than 1,200 permanent jobs.
Coupled with other ventures such as the state's intermodal transportation center and commitments from companies eager to build there, 3,000 new jobs have been guaranteed so far.
Future tenants include the Gillette Co, which will eventually employ 520 in two planned facilities.

Prospects are so bright for the Devens Enterprise Commission, which is overseeing reuse of the property that comprises parts of Ayer, Harvard and Shirley, that the 1993 law creating the commission is being used as a national model for other states that have fallen victim to military downsizing.

Secretary of Defense William Cohen is expected later Monday to recommend closing additional domestic military bases, cutting the 1.4 million-member U.S. armed forces by some 60,000 troops, cutting some warships and shrinking planned fighter jet programs in order to save money for arms modernization as part of the Quadrennial Defense Review.
